extracted.intended_audience: general NPR audience; comedians and comedy writers interested in performance and media controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points for performing stand-up at formal, televised events (e.g., the White House Correspondents' Dinner), covering audience dynamics, content choices, identity-based perspective, and managing backlash. Draws on a comedian's retrospective about what worked, what critics said, and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to your voice / don't apologize
rubrics_metrics.description: "Be true to yourself. Never apologize. Burn it to the ground." (advice a friend gave Michelle Wolf; she also says: "I wouldn't change a single word. I'm very happy with what I said, and I'm glad I stuck to my guns.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist pressure to soften or retract material to placate the room or critics; deliver the material you believe in even if it's polarizing. This is both a strategy for content choices and a stance for handling backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jokes about women's looks
rubrics_metrics.description: "I made a 'conscious effort not to write any jokes about any woman's looks' into the set."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting material about women, deliberately avoid targeting physical appearance; focus on behavior, policy, or actions to reduce perceptions of misogyny and to keep critique substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target behavior and lying rather than appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding the Sarah Sanders joke: "I think it's clear that the joke wasn't about Sarah's looks... it's about the fact that she lies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame jokes around actions, statements, or roles (e.g., lying, being a mouthpiece) rather than surface traits. If material is misunderstood, point back to the intended target (behavior/policy) rather than appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't cater to the room
rubrics_metrics.description: "I wasn't there to 'cater to the room.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not tailor every joke to what you think the specific audience wants to hear at the expense of your comedic point of view; consider the trade-off between short-term applause and staying true to your material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and adapt to 'bad room' characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics cited: "It's a large ballroom. The audience isn't miked so ... the laughs aren't very audible... formal [and] people don't laugh as much when they're dressed up. There's round tables and people are eating or drinking, so by the virtue of a round table, people are partially turned away from you."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how venue layout, lack of close miking, formal dress, round-table seating, and distractions (eating/drinking) reduce audible audience feedback and change timing/pacing. Adjust delivery, punch cadence, and expectations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for televised optics and performative reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: "It's televised and there are all these people that may or may not be able to show genuine reactions... [they're] constantly thinking, 'I need to react in a way that will come off well on TV.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect audience members to modulate reactions for camera/PR reasons; anticipate muted or staged laughter and plan material that can survive or leverage that mediated context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage your identity carefully as a source of perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: "As a woman, I have access to hit women in a way that men might not be able to hit them with jokes... because I'm a woman, I can say things about women, because I know what it's like to be a woman."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lived experience and identity to approach targets in ways that may be more permissible or insightful, but be mindful of nuance so it doesn't read as punching down or reinforce stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of gendered double standards in audience interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think it says a lot about our society that you would immediately think I was talking about her looks rather than her personality... If it was a man you would've been like, 'She's talking about his abilities.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that identical jokes may be read differently depending on the target's gender; plan wording and context to reduce misinterpretation and to foreground the intended critique (abilities/behavior vs. appearance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizers' expectations vs. performer reality
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think sometimes they look at a woman and they think 'Oh, she'll be nice,' and if you've seen any of my comedy you know that I don't — I'm not. I don't pull punches."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for a mismatch between event organizers' assumptions about the performer's style and the performer's actual act. If selected under mistaken assumptions, decide whether to conform or use the opportunity to subvert expectations.
